results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 45 aligned units: the spec-blind summary states the controlling idea of the spec paragraph aligned to it (p01-p44 incl. p16a); the three callouts match no paragraph by design. Note for the author, not a draft fault: spec p03's controlling idea says 'four shared services' while its own evidence and the draft list three services plus the deployment scripts.

Only Checklist ¶1 and Checklist ¶2 are marked two_ideas. ¶1 carries the synthesis/so-what/takeaway plus the eight checks, which are the two clauses of p43's controlling idea; ¶2 carries the callback and the hand-off the spec assigns to p44. Neither is a failure.

Every unit serves a supporting claim: scene and intro set up the question (S1, S3, S4); Cognitive Load -> S1; Assess -> S2; Relieve -> S3; Fracture Planes -> S4; Test a Cut -> S5; anti-patterns answer the disputed view (S1, S4); the worked example applies S2-S5; the AI coda re-tests S1's ownership test; the conclusion synthesizes. No orphan unit.

Every spec evidence item is present with its figures (11->12 days, 4->11 days, 23 of 31, 9 of 11, 3 of 40, 3 of 28, 9->5 days, 14 requests, 19 days). The three quotations are each followed by what they show; all seven tables have a lead-in saying what they hold and Core's list and the worked-example list get a reading paragraph; both figures have captions that state the point. The two unexplained 'At Corvane' cells of the planes table are recorded under flow_is_followable.

All declared transition_in entries (paragraph, section and conclusion level) are expressed at their boundary, e.g. 'That scope showed in two ways' (cause_effect), 'The two decisions have one thing in common' (similarity), 'The second remedy has a condition, though' (contrast), 'It follows that' (cause_effect), 'Even a cut that passes the test has a price' (contrast). In What AI Changes Here ¶1 the section transition is the second sentence, after the label announcement that spec p38 itself requires to open the paragraph; accepted.

results.finding: The opening is a concrete puzzling scenario (the request for two engineers, 11 days before and 12 after), bridged to the reader's own experience and to a disputable thesis; no placeholder, restated question, dictionary definition, dawn-of-man or book-report opening.

The conclusion sorts what holds by how settled it is, joins the two rules into one, and ends on a course of action; no new subtopic, no rephrased-thesis-only ending, no 'in conclusion' opener. Core's details in the closing paragraph are the callback the spec assigns, not new body evidence.

Checklist ¶1 states the synthesis ('They are the same rule seen from two sides ... Headcount enters only after both are settled') and the so-what ('when a request for people or a proposal for a reorganization reaches you, you can ask first ... and decline what the answers do not support'), then the takeaway as eight checks.

Checklist ¶2 returns to the hook: 'Core's request for two engineers can now be read in full', naming the two single-person areas, the complex domain on top of three complicated ones and that nothing was taken away, as the spec's callback declares; the hand-off to flow-and-the-constraint follows.

The cold reader of the opening named the two questions, the thesis and nine topics in exactly the order of the spec's roadmap and the draft's nine body sections (scene, cognitive load, assess, relieve, fracture planes, test a cut, anti-patterns, re-cut, AI).

The cold reader judged the team overloaded ('owns more than it can understand, not one short of hands'), named the signals (areas with a count below two, the incidents, the team's own answer), proposed moving fraud rules or the tax engine along vocabulary, rate-of-change or risk differences after counting crossing changes, and rejected hiring because it does not lower what each member must understand. One nuance of `expected` is weaker: the answer gives the teaching burden on the experts rather than 'raises coordination', which the draft itself states only in the remedies table.

Test a Cut ¶3 states it directly: 'a fracture plane says where a boundary may go, not that it must', followed by four named cases (most changes cross it; a resulting team could not operate its part; nobody is overloaded; the sides stay coupled underneath). The worked example applies it to travel-time estimation and the checklist repeats it.

Cognitive load is glossed at first use in the KEY POINTS callout and Introduction ¶2 and defined and credited to Skelton and Pais's Team Topologies in Cognitive Load ¶1; fracture plane is glossed in Introduction ¶2 ('a seam where the domain, the rate of change or the risk differs') and credited to Team Topologies with its quoted definition in Fracture Planes ¶1; bounded context is defined and credited to Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design, in Fracture Planes ¶3.
